questions.prompt: What is the first thing to check before analysing response times from a load test run?
options: Whether the run was valid: errors, load generator health and whether the intended load was actually applied
The colour scheme of the report
The fastest response
The total number of graphs
questions.explanation: Response times from a run with a failing script, an overloaded load generator or the wrong load are meaningless. Validate the run first.

questions.prompt: Why is the average response time alone a weak summary?
options: It hides the slow tail that a meaningful share of users experience
It is always higher than p99
It cannot be calculated for HTTP
It ignores fast requests
questions.explanation: A few very slow requests barely move the mean, yet those users suffer. Percentiles (p90/p95/p99) describe the tail.

questions.prompt: Very fast responses combined with a high error rate can mean the server is failing quickly rather than performing well.
options: True
False
questions.explanation: Error pages and rejected connections often return in a few milliseconds. Always read response time together with error rate.

questions.prompt: Throughput rises with users up to 200 and then stays flat while response time climbs linearly. What does this pattern usually indicate?
options: A saturated resource: the system is at capacity and extra users just queue
The load generator is too fast
Caching started working
The test is too short
questions.explanation: Flat throughput with growing latency is the queueing signature of a bottleneck. Find which resource saturated at that point.

questions.prompt: Load generator CPU sits at 98% during the test. What follows? Select all that apply.
options: Measured response times may include client-side delays
The applied load may be lower than planned
Add load generators or reduce per-generator load and rerun
The server is definitely the bottleneck
questions.explanation: A saturated generator distorts timing and under-delivers load. You cannot conclude anything about the server until the generator is healthy.

questions.prompt: Two runs of the same test: run A p95 = 820 ms with 0.1% errors; run B p95 = 610 ms with 12% errors (connection refused). Which statement is correct?
options: Run B is not better; its errors make its response times incomparable and point to a capacity or configuration problem
Run B is 25% faster, so it is better
Both runs are equivalent
Run A failed because its p95 is higher
questions.explanation: Refused connections are fast failures that pull percentiles down. Compare runs only when error rates are similar and low.

questions.prompt: p95 is fine for the first 40 minutes of a 2-hour soak test, then rises steadily while throughput stays constant and errors appear after 90 minutes. What is the most likely class of problem, and what evidence would you collect?
options: A resource leak (memory, connections, threads or file handles); collect heap after GC, pool usage and handle counts over time
Insufficient warm-up
Network jitter
Too few virtual users
questions.explanation: Time-dependent degradation at constant load points to accumulation. Trend metrics that should be flat (heap after GC, open connections) will reveal which resource leaks.

questions.prompt: A colleague concludes from a graph that the database caused the slowdown because DB CPU and response time rose together. What should you ask for before agreeing?
options: Evidence of causation: DB query times or wait events, whether DB CPU reached saturation, and whether something else (e.g. a pool or GC) also changed
A bigger graph
The average response time
Nothing; correlation is enough
questions.explanation: Under more load, many metrics rise together. Show that the DB was the constrained resource (saturation, waits, slow queries) before tuning it.

Nearest-rank p95: sort values, take the value at position `ceil(0.95 * n)` (1-based).

hints: Filter successful elapsed values and sort them.

tests.name: Counts and error rate
tests.code:
r = summarise([{'label': 'a', 'elapsed': 100, 'success': True}, {'label': 'a', 'elapsed': 5, 'success': False}, {'label': 'a', 'elapsed': 200, 'success': True}])
assert r['a']['count'] == 3 and r['a']['errors'] == 1 and r['a']['error_pct'] == 33.3, r

tests.name: p95 ignores failures
tests.code:
rows = [{'label': 'x', 'elapsed': v, 'success': True} for v in range(1, 21)] + [{'label': 'x', 'elapsed': 1, 'success': False}]
r = summarise(rows)['x']
assert r['p95'] == 19, r

coding.title: Cut ramp-up and ramp-down
coding.prompt:
Write `steady_state(samples, start, end)` that keeps only samples whose `ts` (seconds) is within `start <= ts < end`, and returns the average `elapsed` of those, rounded to 1 decimal (None if empty).

Example: with samples at ts 0..9 and `start=2, end=8`, only ts 2..7 count.
coding.explanation: Ramp-up includes cold caches and partial load, ramp-down includes partial load; both distort steady-state numbers. A half-open window avoids counting the boundary twice when you split a run into intervals.
hints: Filter with a comprehension and a chained comparison.
Guard against an empty list before dividing.

tests.name: Window is applied
tests.code:
s = [{'ts': t, 'elapsed': 1000 if t < 2 else 100} for t in range(10)]
assert steady_state(s, 2, 8) == 100.0, steady_state(s, 2, 8)

tests.name: Empty window
tests.code: assert steady_state([{'ts': 1, 'elapsed': 5}], 2, 3) is None and steady_state([{'ts': 2, 'elapsed': 5}], 2, 3) == 5.0
